title: Recall bank, Q34–150
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall bank, questions 34–150. Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A boy has darker, coarser, curly pubic hair spreading over the pubis, not yet onto the thighs, and the penis has grown in length. What is his Tanner stage?
questions.exp: Boys: stage 2 = testicular enlargement (4 mL or more, the first sign of puberty) with thin red scrotal skin and sparse straight hair at the base of the penis; stage 3 = penis grows in length, hair darker, coarser and curly; stage 4 = penis grows in breadth with glans development, adult-type hair not reaching the thighs; stage 5 = adult, hair spreads to the thighs.

questions.question: An infant has recurrent bacterial infections without pus, and the umbilical cord fell off late (after 4 weeks). The white cell count is very high. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Leucocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (CD18 integrin defect, autosomal recessive): neutrophils cannot leave the blood, so there is persistent neutrophilia, delayed separation of the umbilical cord, omphalitis, poor wound healing, periodontitis and infections without pus formation. Diagnose by flow cytometry (absent CD18); stem cell transplant cures it.

questions.question: An infant has recurrent otitis media, chronic nappy candidiasis and an unusual infection. Which test is most useful to screen for a T-cell defect?
questions.d: Lymphocyte subsets and T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs)
questions.exp: Persistent candidiasis, opportunistic or severe viral infections and failure to thrive suggest a T-cell or combined defect (SCID). TRECs show recent thymic output (low in SCID, also used in newborn screening); lymphocyte subsets (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19, NK) give the pattern. CH50/AH50 screen complement; NBT/DHR screens for CGD.

questions.question: A child with liver failure is bleeding, with a very high INR. What will stop the bleeding quickly?
questions.d: Fresh frozen plasma (vitamin K is also given but will not correct it)
questions.exp: In liver failure the liver cannot make clotting factors, so vitamin K (given anyway) does not correct the INR. Active bleeding needs FFP (or prothrombin complex), cryoprecipitate for low fibrinogen and platelets if low. A good response to vitamin K would instead suggest cholestasis or vitamin K deficiency.

questions.question: A boy has bleeding with a prolonged APTT and a low factor IX level (haemophilia B). What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Haemophilia B (Christmas disease, X-linked) is treated with recombinant factor IX for bleeds and prophylaxis. Desmopressin works in haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease, not in haemophilia B. Avoid IM injections and NSAIDs.

questions.question: A mother has missed two vaccination appointments for her child and now attends. What should be done?
questions.a: Do not vaccinate because it is too late
questions.b: Give the due vaccines today and explain why they matter
questions.c: Ask her to book a new appointment for next month
questions.d: Call the social worker before giving anything
questions.e: Restart the whole schedule from the beginning
questions.exp: Every contact is a chance to vaccinate: give the overdue vaccines now and follow a catch-up schedule. Interrupted courses are continued, never restarted. Explore the reasons for missed visits without blame; repeated non-attendance alongside other concerns may need safeguarding input.

questions.question: A ventilated neonate suddenly deteriorates and has a pneumothorax. Which ventilator setting most likely caused it?
questions.e: Excessive tidal volume (or high inflation pressure)
questions.exp: Air leaks in ventilated babies come from overdistension (volutrauma or barotrauma): high tidal volumes or pressures, and inadvertent PEEP from too short an expiratory time, especially with stiff RDS lungs. Use volume-targeted ventilation (4–6 mL/kg). A tension pneumothorax needs needle aspiration then a chest drain.

questions.question: A child with cardiomyopathy has glycogen deposits on muscle biopsy. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Glycogen storage with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia is Pompe disease (GSD II), a lysosomal deficiency of acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase). It is treated with enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa). Debranching enzyme deficiency (GSD III) gives hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia and myopathy.

questions.question: A tall boy has lens dislocation and learning difficulties, suggesting homocystinuria. How is it diagnosed?
questions.c: High plasma total homocysteine (with high methionine)
questions.exp: Homocystinuria (CBS deficiency) shows very high plasma homocysteine and high methionine; urine nitroprusside test is positive. Cystine in urine points to cystinuria. Test for pyridoxine responsiveness.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy with Down syndrome wants to start sports. Which statement is correct?
questions.b: He has a risk of atlantoaxial instability, so watch for neck pain or neurological symptoms
questions.c: All children with Down syndrome need a neck X-ray every year
questions.e: He can do any sport with no precautions
questions.exp: Atlantoaxial instability occurs in about 10–20% of children with Down syndrome but is usually symptomless. Routine X-ray screening is no longer advised; parents should know the warning signs (neck pain, head tilt, change in gait, weakness, bladder or bowel change). Exercise is encouraged; some organisations ask for caution with contact sports, diving and gymnastics.

questions.question: A child in status epilepticus has had two doses of rectal diazepam and is still fitting. What is the next step?
questions.exp: After two benzodiazepine doses, give a second-line drug: IV/IO levetiracetam (40 mg/kg) or phenytoin (20 mg/kg); phenobarbital is used in neonates. Then rapid sequence induction if seizures continue.

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl has enlarged lymph nodes in both sides of the neck with no worrying features. When should excision biopsy be considered?
questions.a: If the nodes have not decreased in size after about 4 weeks (or are growing)
questions.b: If they have not decreased in size after 2 weeks
questions.d: If they have not completely resolved after 2 weeks
questions.e: Never; neck nodes in teenagers are always reactive
questions.exp: Reactive nodes are common. Biopsy is indicated for nodes that grow over 2 weeks, fail to shrink after 4–6 weeks or to resolve after 8–12 weeks, or that are over 2 cm, hard, fixed, supraclavicular, or with B symptoms, an abnormal chest X-ray or abnormal blood count.

questions.question: A girl has unilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy with facial oedema and distended neck veins. What should be done first?
questions.a: Chest X-ray to look for a mediastinal mass
questions.c: Bone marrow aspirate under general anaesthesia
questions.d: Excision biopsy of the node under general anaesthesia
questions.exp: Facial swelling and distended neck veins mean superior vena cava syndrome, usually from an anterior mediastinal mass (lymphoma, T-cell leukaemia). A chest X-ray comes first because general anaesthesia or lying flat can cause airway or cardiovascular collapse; diagnose from the least invasive sample possible.

questions.question: A 3-year-old had a cold treated with paracetamol and ibuprofen and improved. Four days later he has itchy, red, ring-shaped wheals on the back. He is well. What should be done?
questions.c: Stop paracetamol and ibuprofen for life
questions.e: Give an oral antihistamine and reassure the parents
questions.exp: Acute urticaria in a young child is most often triggered by a viral infection; drug allergy is less likely. Individual wheals come and go within 24 hours. Treat with a non-sedating antihistamine and reassure. Look for features of anaphylaxis, or of serum sickness-like reaction (joint swelling, fever) or erythema multiforme (fixed target lesions).

questions.question: A child with systemic JIA becomes acutely unwell with persistent fever, falling ESR and platelets, very high ferritin and raised liver enzymes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.b: A normal flare of systemic JIA
questions.exp: Macrophage activation syndrome (secondary HLH) is a life-threatening complication of systemic JIA: continuous fever, hepatosplenomegaly, very high ferritin, falling ESR (fibrinogen consumption), cytopenias, raised transaminases, triglycerides and LDH, and coagulopathy. Treat urgently with IV methylprednisolone, ciclosporin and/or anakinra.

questions.question: A child has acute weakness of both legs, urinary retention and a sensory level on the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A sensory level with bilateral weakness and bladder or bowel involvement localises to the spinal cord. Transverse myelitis is often post-infectious. Get an urgent MRI of the spine to exclude cord compression, then treat with high-dose steroids. Guillain–Barré has no sensory level.

questions.question: A child has polyuria and polydipsia, with low potassium, low chloride, low magnesium and metabolic alkalosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Gitelman syndrome: salt wasting from the distal convoluted tubule, with hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia and low urinary calcium, normal blood pressure. RTA gives acidosis; Liddle and hyperaldosteronism cause hypertension.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl was stung on the finger by a scorpion. She has local pain and redness only, with a normal examination otherwise. What should be done?
questions.a: Apply a tight tourniquet to the finger
questions.e: Analgesia (including local anaesthetic) and observation; no antivenom
questions.exp: Most scorpion stings cause only local pain: treat with cold compresses, oral analgesia or a local anaesthetic block, and observe for several hours for systemic signs (sweating, salivation, vomiting, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary oedema). Antivenom is for systemic envenomation. Tourniquets and incisions are harmful.

questions.question: A short girl has a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples and puffy hands and feet at birth. Which heart lesion is most typical?
questions.b: Bicuspid aortic valve or coarctation of the aorta
questions.exp: Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaic): short stature, webbed neck, lymphoedema at birth, wide-spaced nipples, ovarian failure, horseshoe kidney and left-sided heart lesions (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation), with a later risk of aortic dilatation. Diagnose by karyotype in any short girl; treat with GH and oestrogen.

questions.question: A toddler has typical cyanotic breath-holding spells. What is the management?
questions.d: Reassure the parents and check for iron deficiency
questions.exp: Breath-holding spells are benign and stop by 5–6 years. Reassure; advise calm handling and not rewarding the behaviour. Check a full blood count and ferritin (iron helps even without anaemia), and do an ECG if atypical.

questions.question: A child has a focal neurological deficit, and brain imaging shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the temporal lobe (brain abscess). Which underlying condition is most likely?
questions.exp: Brain abscess in children is linked to cyanotic heart disease with right-to-left shunt (such as tetralogy of Fallot: blood bypasses the lung filter), sinusitis, otitis media and mastoiditis, penetrating head injury and immunodeficiency. Treat with prolonged IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole) and drainage if needed.

questions.question: A child with cystic fibrosis has a raised bilirubin. Which investigation is first?
questions.exp: CF liver disease (focal biliary cirrhosis, portal hypertension), gallstones and fatty liver can cause raised bilirubin and liver enzymes. Ultrasound shows liver texture, the biliary tree, gallstones and spleen size. Ursodeoxycholic acid is often used.

questions.question: A child has severe eczema, recurrent skin "cold" abscesses, pneumonias with pneumatoceles, retained baby teeth and a very high IgE. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (STAT3): eczema from early infancy, cold staphylococcal abscesses, recurrent pneumonia with pneumatoceles, coarse face, retained primary teeth, scoliosis and fractures, and very high IgE with eosinophilia. Wiskott–Aldrich has thrombocytopenia with small platelets.

questions.question: An 8 kg infant has supraventricular tachycardia and is shocked. What is the treatment?
questions.c: Synchronised DC cardioversion at 8 J (1 J/kg), increasing to 16 J
questions.exp: Unstable SVT is treated with synchronised cardioversion 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg, under sedation (adenosine can be tried first only if IV access is immediately available). Unsynchronised defibrillation (4 J/kg) is for pulseless VT or VF.

questions.question: A mother with breast cancer asks for her 14-year-old daughter to be tested for the BRCA gene. Which ethical principle argues against testing now?
questions.b: Respect for the daughter's future autonomy
questions.exp: Predictive testing for adult-onset conditions with no treatment or screening benefit in childhood (BRCA, Huntington) is normally delayed until the young person can decide for herself, protecting her future autonomy (and confidentiality). Testing is offered in childhood when results change care in childhood (familial polyposis, MEN2).

questions.question: A neonate is in shock with capillary refill over 3 seconds, cold extremities and mottling despite fluids. Which drug is preferred?
questions.exp: Cold, fluid-refractory shock is treated with adrenaline as the first-line inotrope (via peripheral or central line), with careful volume management. Noradrenaline suits warm, vasodilated shock. Milrinone and dobutamine help low-output states with normal blood pressure.

questions.question: A baby has a growing haemangioma on the upper eyelid that partly covers the eye. What is the treatment?
questions.b: Observe; it will regress by itself
questions.c: Oral propranolol, with urgent ophthalmology review
questions.exp: An infantile haemangioma near the eye can cause amblyopia (occlusion, astigmatism) and needs treatment early. Oral propranolol (1–3 mg/kg/day, monitoring for hypoglycaemia, bradycardia and bronchospasm) is first-line for problematic haemangiomas; surgery is for residual tissue later.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell anaemia suddenly develops hemiplegia. What should be done?
questions.b: Wait for an MRI next week before treatment
questions.d: Urgent exchange transfusion (after rapid imaging), without delay
questions.exp: Acute stroke in sickle cell disease is an emergency: give oxygen, fluids and urgent imaging (CT/MRI), and start exchange transfusion as soon as possible to bring HbS below 30%; if exchange is delayed, give a simple top-up transfusion first. Long-term regular transfusion prevents recurrence; TCD screening prevents first strokes.

questions.question: A child has recurrent skin abscesses and abscesses in internal organs (liver, lung). Which test diagnoses the likely immunodeficiency?
questions.exp: Chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase defect, mostly X-linked) causes catalase-positive infections (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Burkholderia), with abscesses and granulomas. The DHR test (or older NBT test) shows absent oxidative burst. Prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole, itraconazole, interferon gamma; cure by stem cell transplant.

questions.question: Which fracture is most specific for non-accidental injury in an infant?
questions.a: Distal radius buckle fracture after a fall
questions.b: Spiral tibial fracture in a walking toddler
questions.d: Metaphyseal (corner or bucket-handle) fracture of a long bone
questions.e: Clavicle fracture after a difficult birth
questions.exp: Highly specific fractures: classic metaphyseal lesions (from shaking or twisting), posterior rib fractures, scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures, and multiple fractures of different ages. A toddler's fracture (spiral tibia in a walking child) and birth-related clavicle fractures are usually accidental.

questions.question: A boy has haematuria and proteinuria. Several males on his mother's side developed kidney failure early in life, and some are deaf. What does a renal biopsy show?
questions.c: Complement C3 deposits in a tram-track pattern only
questions.d: Glomerular basement membrane abnormalities (thinning, thickening and splitting) from a type IV collagen defect
questions.e: Linear IgG deposition with lung haemorrhage
questions.exp: Alport syndrome (mostly X-linked, COL4A5): haematuria from childhood, later proteinuria and progressive kidney failure in males, sensorineural hearing loss and eye changes (anterior lenticonus). Electron microscopy shows a "basket-weave" split and thickened GBM. ACE inhibitors slow progression.

questions.question: A newborn has a heart rate of 70/min and is gasping (respiratory rate 40). What should be done first?
questions.exp: A heart rate under 100 with apnoea or gasping needs effective ventilation (inflation breaths then ventilation breaths). Start chest compressions (3:1) only if the heart rate stays under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

questions.question: A newborn has SpO2 95% and a heart rate of 90/min, but is breathing only 4 times a minute. What is the next step?
questions.d: Positive pressure ventilation with air (21% oxygen)
questions.exp: Apnoea with a heart rate under 100 needs ventilation. Term babies are resuscitated starting with air; oxygen is added according to pre-ductal saturation targets. Free-flow oxygen does not help a baby who is not breathing.

questions.question: A child's spirometry shows a low FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio (92%). Which condition fits best?
questions.exp: A restrictive pattern (low FVC and total lung capacity with a normal or high FEV1/FVC) is seen in interstitial lung disease, chest wall disorders (scoliosis) and neuromuscular weakness. Obstructive disease (asthma, CF, bronchiolitis obliterans) gives a low FEV1/FVC ratio.

questions.question: A child has tyrosinaemia type 1 with raised succinylacetone and tyrosine. What is the treatment?
questions.c: Nitisinone with a diet low in tyrosine and phenylalanine
questions.exp: Nitisinone (NTBC) blocks the pathway upstream, stopping the toxic metabolites (succinylacetone) that damage the liver and kidneys; tyrosine then rises, so a low tyrosine and phenylalanine diet is needed. Screen for hepatocellular carcinoma (AFP, imaging). Liver transplant if nitisinone fails.

questions.question: A child has rheumatoid factor-positive, ANA-negative polyarticular JIA. How often should eye screening for uveitis be done?
questions.e: Only if the eye becomes red
questions.exp: Chronic anterior uveitis in JIA is painless and symptomless, so screening by slit lamp is needed. Highest risk: ANA-positive oligoarticular or polyarticular JIA starting under 7 years (every 3 months). RF-positive polyarticular and systemic JIA are low risk (every 12 months).

questions.question: A boy has right hip pain and a limp after a cold. He is afebrile; WCC is 6,000 and ESR 15. Ultrasound shows small effusions in both hips. What is the management?
questions.exp: Transient synovitis: a well child (3–10 years), often after a viral infection, with a limp, no or low fever, and normal inflammatory markers. Treat with rest and NSAIDs; it settles in days. Kocher criteria for septic arthritis: fever over 38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR over 40, WCC over 12,000 (plus CRP over 20).

questions.question: A child has had a febrile convulsion. Which factor increases the risk of later epilepsy?
questions.a: A family history of febrile convulsions
questions.c: Fever above 39°C at the time of the seizure
questions.e: Age 18 months at the first seizure
questions.exp: Risk of later epilepsy after febrile seizures is low (about 2%), higher with neurodevelopmental abnormality, complex febrile seizures (focal, over 15 minutes, or repeated within 24 hours) and a family history of EPILEPSY. Young age, low fever and a family history of febrile seizures predict RECURRENCE of febrile seizures, not epilepsy.

questions.question: A 15-year-old with autism has severe aggressive behaviour despite behavioural support. Which drug can be used?
questions.exp: Risperidone and aripiprazole are licensed for irritability and aggression in autism when behavioural approaches are not enough; monitor weight, metabolic effects and prolactin. Methylphenidate and atomoxetine treat co-existing ADHD; melatonin helps sleep.

questions.question: A doctor looks back at records to compare hyponatraemia in children who received a certain IV fluid and children who did not. What type of study is this?
questions.exp: A cohort study groups people by EXPOSURE (fluid or no fluid) and compares OUTCOMES (hyponatraemia); it can be retrospective using existing records. A case–control study starts from the outcome (children with and without hyponatraemia) and looks back at exposures. In an RCT, the investigator assigns the fluid by randomisation.

questions.question: A child has a pulseless cardiac arrest, and the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the first action?
questions.a: Defibrillation at 4 J/kg as soon as possible, with CPR until the defibrillator is ready
questions.exp: VF and pulseless VT are shockable: start CPR, shock (4 J/kg) as soon as possible, then 2 minutes of CPR, rhythm check. Adrenaline (10 micrograms/kg) and amiodarone (5 mg/kg) are given after the third shock. Synchronised shocks are for tachycardias with a pulse.

questions.question: A girl has weakness of both legs (power 4/5), low tone and reduced reflexes, and cannot walk without support. There is no ptosis or fatigability. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Proximal (hip and shoulder girdle) weakness with low tone and reduced reflexes in a girl suggests a limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (many genes; CK raised). Duchenne affects boys; myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with ptosis; myotonic dystrophy has facial weakness, ptosis and myotonia; CP has increased tone.

questions.question: An infant of a diabetic mother was born vaginally after shoulder dystocia. He has an asymmetric Moro reflex, a claw hand and ptosis on the same side. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Klumpke palsy (lower brachial plexus, C8–T1): weak hand muscles (claw hand) with a preserved grasp of the upper arm, and Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis) if T1 sympathetic fibres are injured. Erb palsy (C5–C6) gives the "waiter's tip" posture with a preserved grasp. Large babies of diabetic mothers are at risk from shoulder dystocia.

questions.question: An unvaccinated child has fever for 2 days and a papulovesicular rash. Which isolation precautions are needed in hospital?
questions.exp: Varicella spreads by the airborne route and by direct contact with vesicle fluid, so it needs a negative-pressure room with airborne and contact precautions until all lesions have crusted. Measles also needs airborne precautions; staff should be immune.

questions.question: A child with tetralogy of Fallot has a hypercyanotic spell. What is the initial treatment?
questions.exp: First steps: calm the child, knee-chest position (or hold knees to chest in an infant) to raise systemic resistance and reduce right-to-left shunting, and give oxygen. If the spell continues: morphine, fluid bolus, propranolol or esmolol, bicarbonate for acidosis, and phenylephrine.

questions.question: A short child has a systolic murmur in the right second intercostal space (supravalvular aortic stenosis), a friendly personality and an elfin face. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion including elastin): supravalvular aortic stenosis (heard at the right upper sternal edge), peripheral pulmonary stenosis, hypercalcaemia, elfin face, overfriendly personality and learning difficulty. Noonan syndrome has pulmonary stenosis at the LEFT upper sternal edge.

questions.question: A 10-day-old baby has seizures and irritability from meningitis. Which organism is most likely?
questions.exp: Group B streptococcus is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis (early and late onset, up to 3 months), followed by E. coli; Listeria is less common. Empirical treatment under 1 month: IV cefotaxime (or ceftriaxone if not jaundiced) plus amoxicillin to cover Listeria.

questions.question: A child has bloody diarrhoea and crampy abdominal pain with no fever. Which organism is most likely?
questions.exp: STEC typically causes bloody diarrhoea with severe cramps and little or no fever, and 5–15% of children develop haemolytic uraemic syndrome about a week later (check FBC, film and creatinine). Avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs. Shigella usually causes high fever and can cause seizures.

questions.question: A child's height has fallen below the 3rd centile, but his weight is normal (he looks plump for his height). Which group of causes is most likely?
questions.b: Endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism or growth hormone deficiency
questions.exp: When height falls more than weight (short and relatively overweight), think endocrine: hypothyroidism (high TSH, low T4), GH deficiency, Cushing syndrome. When weight falls first and more than height (thin and short), think nutritional or chronic disease: coeliac disease, IBD, CF, poor intake.

questions.question: A preterm baby has an intraventricular haemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix. What grade is it (Papile)?
questions.exp: Papile grading: 1 = germinal matrix haemorrhage only; 2 = blood in the ventricle without dilatation; 3 = blood with ventricular dilatation; 4 = periventricular haemorrhagic infarction in the brain tissue. Grades 3–4 carry high risks of hydrocephalus and cerebral palsy.

questions.question: A cyanosed newborn in shock has a huge globular ("wall-to-wall") heart on chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Ebstein anomaly (downward displacement of the tricuspid valve, linked to maternal lithium) causes severe tricuspid regurgitation and a huge right atrium, giving massive cardiomegaly, cyanosis from right-to-left atrial shunting, and WPW in about 20%. ToF is boot-shaped and small; TGA is "egg on a string"; obstructed TAPVR has a small heart.

questions.question: A father has X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets. What proportion of his daughters will be affected?
questions.exp: In X-linked dominant inheritance, an affected father passes his X chromosome to every daughter (all affected) and his Y to every son (none affected). An affected mother passes it to 50% of her children of either sex.

questions.question: A baby of an HBsAg-positive mother receives hepatitis B immunoglobulin and the first vaccine dose at birth. What is a suitable schedule for the remaining monovalent vaccine doses?
questions.b: 2, 4 and 6 months without a birth dose
questions.exp: After HBIG and vaccine within 12 hours of birth, complete the series: monovalent vaccine at 0, 1 and 6 months, or as part of the hexavalent vaccine at 2, 4 and 6 months (a 4-dose schedule including birth). Test for HBsAg and anti-HBs at 9–12 months.

questions.question: A child with recurrent otitis media and a retracted eardrum now has a persistent, foul-smelling ear discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cholesteatoma (skin growing into the middle ear from a retraction pocket) causes painless, foul-smelling, persistent discharge, conductive hearing loss and white debris in the attic. It erodes the ossicles and can cause facial palsy, meningitis or brain abscess. Refer to ENT for surgery.

questions.question: Which antiepileptic drugs can make myoclonic seizures worse?
questions.b: Phenytoin and carbamazepine (and lamotrigine in some)
questions.exp: Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin) and vigabatrin, gabapentin and tiagabine can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures, as in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; lamotrigine may worsen myoclonus in some. Valproate and levetiracetam are the drugs of choice for myoclonic epilepsies.

questions.question: A girl tells her teacher that her parents force her to watch pornographic videos. What should the teacher do?
questions.a: Listen, reassure her, and report it promptly to the child protection lead or authorities
questions.b: Wait until she says it again
questions.c: Investigate first by asking the parents
questions.e: Ignore it unless there are physical signs
questions.exp: Exposing a child to pornography is sexual abuse. The person told should listen, not ask leading questions, not promise confidentiality, record her words, and refer the same day to the designated safeguarding lead or children's services. Do not confront the parents, which may put the child at risk.

questions.question: How is Hirschsprung disease confirmed?
questions.e: Rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells
questions.exp: A rectal suction biopsy showing no ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve fibres (increased acetylcholinesterase, absent calretinin) confirms Hirschsprung disease. A contrast enema can show the transition zone, and anorectal manometry shows an absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex.

questions.question: A child has a blunt abdominal injury during sport. He has periumbilical pain but is conscious and haemodynamically stable. Which investigation should be done?
questions.a: Serum amylase and urine tests only
questions.d: CT of the abdomen with IV contrast
questions.exp: In a haemodynamically stable child with significant blunt abdominal trauma, contrast CT is the investigation of choice for solid organ, pancreatic and bowel injuries (look for handlebar marks, seat-belt sign). Unstable children go to theatre. Amylase can be normal early in pancreatic injury.

questions.question: A child is bitten on the index finger by a snake. There is local swelling only. What is the management?
questions.c: Admit for observation, immobilise the limb, and give antivenom only if envenomation progresses
questions.e: Give antivenom straight away to all
questions.exp: Many bites cause no or local envenomation. Admit for at least 24 hours, immobilise the limb, mark the swelling, and monitor clotting (20-minute whole blood clotting test), renal function and neurology. Antivenom is given for systemic envenomation (bleeding, coagulopathy, neurotoxicity, shock) or rapidly spreading swelling. Tourniquets and incisions are harmful.

questions.question: A child is rescued from a fire with no skin burns but signs of smoke inhalation. He is intubated, and the blood gas shows metabolic acidosis. What is the most likely cause of the acidosis?
questions.c: Carbon monoxide (and cyanide) poisoning causing tissue hypoxia
questions.e: Simple hypoxia from airway swelling only
questions.exp: CO binds haemoglobin (carboxyhaemoglobin) and cyanide blocks cellular respiration, both causing lactic acidosis despite a normal PaO2; pulse oximetry is falsely normal in CO poisoning. Give 100% oxygen and measure COHb by co-oximetry; consider hydroxocobalamin for cyanide with severe lactic acidosis.

questions.question: A child with recurrent otitis and sinusitis has a brother with cystic fibrosis. Two sweat chloride tests are 40 mmol/L. He is otherwise well. Which investigation will help reach the diagnosis?
questions.d: Nasal brushing for ciliary studies only
questions.exp: Sweat chloride of 60 or more is diagnostic of CF; 30–59 is intermediate. With intermediate results, extended CFTR mutation analysis (and nasal potential difference if needed) can confirm CF or a CFTR-related disorder. IRT is a newborn screening test and is unreliable later.

questions.question: A 7-month-old is travelling to an area with a measles outbreak. What is the measles vaccination plan?
questions.a: One dose before travel and no more
questions.c: Doses at 12 and 18 months only, no extra dose
questions.d: An extra MMR dose before travel, then the routine two doses from 12 months
questions.e: MMR is contraindicated before 12 months in all cases
questions.exp: Infants aged 6–11 months can get an early MMR dose before travel or during an outbreak; it does not count towards the routine course because maternal antibodies may blunt the response, so two further doses are given from 12 months (12–15 months and 4–6 years, or as in the local schedule).

questions.question: A short girl with no other obvious features is being investigated. Which test must be included?
questions.exp: Turner syndrome may present with short stature alone, without the classic features. Every girl with unexplained short stature (or delayed puberty) needs a karyotype, along with thyroid function, coeliac screen, IGF-1 and bone age.

questions.question: A teenager has high blood pressure with attacks of sweating, headache, palpitations and flushing. Which investigation is needed?
questions.a: Plasma free or urinary metanephrines and catecholamines
questions.exp: Phaeochromocytoma or paraganglioma causes sustained or paroxysmal hypertension with headache, sweating and palpitations. Screen with plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines, then image (CT/MRI, MIBG). Children often have bilateral or extra-adrenal tumours and genetic syndromes (VHL, MEN2, SDH, NF1). Alpha-blockade before surgery.

questions.question: A child has a high blood pressure reading on two occasions. What is the next step?
questions.b: Start a beta-blocker and DASH diet together
questions.d: Confirm with repeated measurements and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
questions.exp: Diagnose hypertension only after repeated readings on 3 occasions with the right cuff size; ambulatory BP monitoring confirms it and excludes white-coat hypertension. Then evaluate for secondary causes (more likely in young children and with high readings), start lifestyle (DASH diet, exercise) and medication if needed.

questions.question: A child has abdominal pain, arthritis and a purpuric rash on the legs and buttocks. Which finding supports the diagnosis of Henoch–Schönlein purpura?
questions.b: A raised serum IgA (with a normal platelet count)
questions.exp: HSP (IgA vasculitis) is a clinical diagnosis: palpable purpura with normal platelets, plus abdominal pain, arthritis or renal involvement. Serum IgA is raised in about half; biopsy shows IgA deposits. Complement is normal. Monitor urine and BP for 6–12 months for nephritis.
